source_text: Et quoniam tria sunt, quibus homo constat: spiritus. anima et corpus, quae rursus duo dicuntur, quia saepe anima simul cum spiritu nominatur — pars enim quaedam eiusdem rationalis, qua carent bestiae, spiritus dicitur — principale nostrum spiritus est; deinde uita, qua coniungimur corpori, anima dicitur; postremo ipsum corpus, quoniam uisibile est, ultimum nostrum est. haec autem omnis creatura ingemescit et parturit usque nunc; dedit tamen primitias spiritus, quia credidit deo et bonae iam uoluntatis est. hic enim spiritus etiam mens uocatur, de quo dicit apostolus: mente seruio legi dei, qui item alio loco dicit: testis est enim mihi deus, cui seruio in spiritu meo. anima uero, cum carnalia bona adhuc adpetit, caro nominatur et resistit spiritui non natura, sed consuetudine peccatorum. unde dicitur: mente seruio legi dei, carne autem legi peccati. quae consuetudo in naturam uersa est secundum generationem mortalem peccato primi hominis. ideoque scriptum est: et nos aliquando fuimus natura filii irae, id est uindictae, per quam factum est, ut seruiamus legi peccati. est autem animae natura perfecta, cum spiritui suo subditur et cum sequitur sequentem deum. ideo animalis homo non percipit quae sunt spiritus dei. sed non tam cito anima subiugatur spiritui ad bonam operationem, quam cito spiritus deo ad ueram fidem et bonam uoluntatem, sed aliquando tardius eius inpetus, quo in carnalia et temporalia diffluit, refrenatur. sed quoniam et ipsa mundatur, recipiens stabilitatem naturae suae dominante spiritu, quod sibi caput est, cuius capitis caput est Christus. non est desperandum etiam corpus restitui naturae propriae; sed utique non tam cito quam anima, sicut neque. anima tam cito quam spiritus, sed tempore oportuno in nouissima tuba, cum mortui resurgent incorrupti et nos inmutabimur. et ideo credimus et in carnis resurrectionem, non tantum quia reparatur anima, quae nunc propter carnales affectiones caro nominatur, sed haec etiam uisibilis caro, quae naturaliter est caro, cuius nomen anima non propter naturam, sed propter affectiones carnales accepit, haec ergo uisibilis quae proprie dicitur caro sine dubitatione credenda est resurgere. uidetur enim Paulus apostolus eam tamquam digito ostendere, cum dicit: oportet corruptibile hoc induere incorruptionem. cum enim dicit \'hoc\', in eam quasi digitum intendit. quod autem uisibile est, id potest digito ostendi, quoniam potest etiam anima corruptibilis dici; nam. uitiis morum ipsa corrumpitur. et mortale hoc induere inmortalitatem cum legitur, eadem significatur uisibilis caro, quia in eam identidem uelut digitus intenditur. potest enim et anima sicut corruptibilis propter morum uitia, ita etiam mortalis dici. mors quippe animae est apostatare a deo: quod primum eius peccatum in paradiso sacris litteris continetur.
thought_title: The three parts of the human person and the resurrection of the visible body
orientation: Augustine has just finished the article on the forgiveness of sins and now explains the resurrection of the body by distinguishing spirit, soul, and body in the human person.
pass_a_gloss: And since three [things] are, [by] which man consists: spirit. soul and body, which again two are said, because often [the] soul together with [the] spirit is named — [a] part for indeed [of] the same rational [thing], [by] which beasts lack, [the] spirit is called — [the] principal [thing] of ours [the] spirit is; then [the] life, [by] which we are joined to [the] body, [the] soul is called; lastly [the] body itself, since visible it is, [the] last [thing] of ours it is. But this whole creation groans and travails until now; it gave however [the] firstfruits of [the] spirit, because it believed God and of good now will it is. For this spirit also [the] mind is called, about which says [the] apostle: with [the] mind I serve [the] law of God, who likewise in another place says: witness for is to me God, whom I serve in my spirit. [The] soul however, when carnal good [things] still it desires, [the] flesh is called and resists [the] spirit not [by] nature, but [by] custom of sins. Whence it is said: with [the] mind I serve [the] law of God, with [the] flesh however [the] law of sin. Which custom into nature has been turned according to [the] generation mortal [by the] sin of [the] first man. And therefore it is written: and we once were by nature children of wrath, that is of vengeance, through which it has come to pass, that we serve [the] law of sin. But is [the] nature of [the] soul perfect, when to its spirit it is subjected and when it follows [the] following God. Therefore [the] animal man does not perceive [the things] which are of [the] spirit of God. But not so quickly [the] soul is subjected to [the] spirit for good operation, as quickly [the] spirit to God for true faith and good will, but sometimes more slowly its impulse, [by] which into carnal and temporal [things] it flows away, is restrained. But since also [the] soul itself is cleansed, receiving [the] stability of its own nature [with the] spirit ruling, which to it [the] head is, of which head [the] head is Christ. [It is] not to be despaired [that] also [the] body [is] to be restored to [its] own nature; but certainly not so quickly as [the] soul, just as neither [the] soul so quickly as [the] spirit, but [at the] time opportune in [the] last trumpet, when [the] dead will rise incorruptible and we will be changed. And therefore we believe also in [the] resurrection of [the] flesh, not only because [the] soul is repaired, which now on account of carnal affections [the] flesh is called, but this also visible flesh, which naturally is flesh, whose name [the] soul not on account of nature, but on account of carnal affections has received, this therefore visible [flesh] which properly is called flesh without doubt is to be believed to rise. For [the] apostle Paul seems it as with [a] finger to point out, when he says: [it] behooves this corruptible [thing] to put on incorruption. For when he says 'this', into it as [with] a finger he points. But what visible is, that can with [a] finger be pointed out, since can also [the] soul corruptible be called; for. by [the] vices of morals itself it is corrupted. And this mortal [thing] to put on immortality when it is read, [the] same is signified visible flesh, because into it repeatedly as [a] finger is pointed. For can also [the] soul just as corruptible on account of [the] vices of morals, so also mortal be called. [The] death indeed of [the] soul is to apostatize from God: which first its sin in paradise [in the] sacred writings is contained.

choices.why: Glossary term for the highest part of the human person; kept literal to preserve the tripartite distinction Augustine is making.
Glossary term for the life that joins spirit to body; literal rendering preserves the distinction from spirit.
Glossary term for human flesh, especially the visible body; kept literal to preserve the contrast with soul and spirit.
Glossary term for the future rising of the visible flesh; 'body' is the required rendering, not 'flesh'.
Literal rendering of 'animalis' as 'animal' preserves the Pauline contrast between the natural and spiritual person; 'human being' for 'homo' is inclusive.
Literal rendering of the Pauline phrase; 'children of wrath' is the standard English idiom for 'filii irae'.

pass_b_english: And since there are three things of which a human being consists—spirit, soul, and body—these are again spoken of as two, because the soul is often named together with the spirit. For a certain part of the same soul, the rational part, which beasts lack, is called spirit. Our principal part is the spirit; next, the life by which we are joined to the body is called soul; finally, the body itself, since it is visible, is our last part. Now this whole creation groans and is in labor until now (Romans 8:22); yet it has given the firstfruits of the spirit, because it has believed God and is already of good will. For this spirit is also called mind, about which the apostle says: “With my mind I serve the law of God” (Romans 7:25). He also says in another place: “For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit” (Romans 1:9). But the soul, when it still desires fleshly goods, is called flesh and resists the spirit—not by nature, but by the habit of sins. Hence it is said: “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin” (Romans 7:25). This habit has been turned into nature through the mortal generation brought about by the sin of the first human being. Therefore it is written: “And we too were once by nature children of wrath” (Ephesians 2:3), that is, of punishment, through which it came about that we serve the law of sin. But the nature of the soul is perfect when it is subjected to its own spirit and when it follows the spirit that follows God. Therefore the animal human being does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 2:14). But the soul is not subjected to the spirit for good action as quickly as the spirit is subjected to God for true faith and good will; rather, its impulse, by which it flows away into fleshly and temporal things, is sometimes reined in more slowly. But since the soul itself is also cleansed, receiving the stability of its own nature when the spirit rules—the spirit, which is its head, whose head is Christ—we must not despair that the body too will be restored to its own nature. But certainly not as quickly as the soul, just as the soul is not restored as quickly as the spirit, but at the proper time, at the last trumpet, when the dead will rise incorruptible and we will be changed (1 Corinthians 15:52). And therefore we believe also in the resurrection of the body—not only because the soul is repaired, which is now called flesh because of fleshly affections, but also this visible flesh, which is flesh by nature, whose name the soul received not because of nature but because of fleshly affections. This visible flesh, then, which is properly called flesh, must without doubt be believed to rise. For the apostle Paul seems to point at it as with a finger when he says: “This corruptible must put on incorruption” (1 Corinthians 15:53). For when he says “this,” he points his finger, as it were, at it. Now what is visible can be pointed at with a finger, since the soul can also be called corruptible; for it is corrupted by the vices of morals. And when we read, “and this mortal must put on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:53), the same visible flesh is meant, because the finger is again, as it were, pointed at it. For the soul can also be called mortal, just as it can be called corruptible because of the vices of morals. Indeed, the death of the soul is to apostatize from God: its first sin in paradise is contained in the sacred writings.

problems.quote: For a certain part of that same rational nature, which beasts lack, is called spirit.
problems.source_quote: pars enim quaedam eiusdem rationalis, qua carent bestiae, spiritus dicitur
problems.why: eiusdem rationalis is genitive singular agreeing with animae: 'of the same soul's rational part', not 'rational nature'.
problems.fix: For a certain part of the same soul, the rational part, which beasts lack, is called spirit.
problems.ruling: eiusdem refers back to animae (soul), not natura; 'rationalis' is substantive genitive singular 'of the rational [part/soul]', not 'rational nature'.

edits.old: For a certain part of that same rational nature, which beasts lack, is called spirit.
edits.new: For a certain part of the same soul, the rational part, which beasts lack, is called spirit.

fixed: Corrected: 'eiusdem rationalis' is genitive singular agreeing with 'animae' (the soul), not 'rational nature'; the English now reads 'a certain part of the same soul, the rational part'.

last_rejected.quote: Now this whole creation groans and is in labor until now (Romans 8:22)
last_rejected.source_quote: haec autem omnis creatura ingemescit et parturit usque nunc
last_rejected.why: Augustine quotes Rom 8:22-23 but English cites only v.22; 'dedit tamen primitias spiritus' is v.23.
last_rejected.fix: Now this whole creation groans and is in labor until now; yet it has given the firstfruits of the spirit (Romans 8:22-23).
last_rejected.ruling: 'usque nunc' matches Rom 8:22; 'primitias spiritus' follows as author's own statement, not necessarily part of the quote.

last_rejected.why: 'Animalis' means 'natural/carnal' (1 Cor 2:14), not 'animal-like'; this misrepresents Paul's Greek ψυχικός.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Animalis homo' translates the Latin Vulgate rendering of ψυχικός; 'animal human being' is a standard literal rendering.

last_rejected.quote: when it follows the spirit that follows God
last_rejected.why: Ambiguous: 'sequentem deum' means God whom one follows, not 'the spirit that follows God'.
last_rejected.ruling: 'cum sequitur sequentem deum' = 'follows [the spirit] following God'; English correctly captures the chain: soul follows spirit following God.
